Guilty? I mean... I don't know if guilt is the right word. Maybe? I don't really sit around blaming myself for things, I don't think. Mostly I just feel tired. Like, bone-tired. It reminds me of this one time I had to replace the entire subfloor in this Victorian house over in West Chester. Built in 1890-something. Everything is farmed fast, you know? Fast-growth pine is basically just a sponge. It warps if you even look at it wrong. 

Anyway, I spent three weeks under that house, just breathing in century-old dust and rat droppings. I had this respirator, but the straps kept digging into my neck. Left this red welt that stung every time I showered... I used that Lava soap back then, the one with the pumice in it? Cuts right through the grease and sap, but man, it takes a layer of skin with it if you scrub too hard. 

But yeah... what were we talking about? Blaming myself? No, I don't really think I do that. It's more just... everything's just heavy.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Energy? No. Not even close. It's like... by midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling lumber all day, you know? Just heavy. And even after a full night in bed, I can barely push through measuring or cutting, or even returning calls without feeling totally wiped out. 

It's funny you mention energy, though, because it makes me think of my old compressor. I had this big, red 20-gallon DeWalt compressor for years. Bought it at a pawn shop over in Camden. Guy running the place had a glass eye, I swear. It didn't track right when he looked at you. Anyway, that compressor was a beast, but the regulator valve started sticking on it. You'd turn it on, and it would just hum... this low, vibrating hum that rattled your teeth, but it wouldn't build any pressure. Just sat there using up electricity. I took the whole housing apart trying to fix it. There's this little rubber O-ring inside the manifold that gets brittle if you don't drain the tank regularly. People never drain their tanks, you know? You're supposed to open the petcock at the bottom after every use to let the condensation out, otherwise the inside just rusts to pieces. I knew a guy who had a tank actually blow out on him because the bottom rusted through. Sounded like a shotgun went off in his garage. Blew a hole right through drywall... 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, my energy. Yeah, it's just gone. I just feel wiped out all the time. Like that old compressor, just humming but not doing anything.

Suicide? No, no. I haven't... I don't want to kill myself or anything like that. I just... I don't know, sometimes I just wish I could go to sleep and not have to wake up and do it all over again, you know? 

Speaking of sleeping, I bought this new mattress a couple years ago. One of those memory foam things they ship to you in a box. But, uh... yeah. I'm not thinking about killing myself. I just... I'm just so tired of feeling like this.

How long? Well, let's see... it's been going on since I took on the studio mortgage. That was a little over two years ago. I'd say about two years and two months now. 

I remember because I signed the papers right around the time the transmission went out on my brother's Ford. He's got this 2015 F-150, the one with the aluminum body. They made a huge deal out of that when it came out, you know, "military-grade aluminum alloy" or whatever the commercials said. Supposed to make the truck lighter so it gets better gas mileage, but then they put these tiny little EcoBoost engines in them. Sure, they got twin turbos, but it's still just a V6 trying to pull a full-size truck. Anyway, his transmission started slipping going from third to fourth gear. Just a hard clunk every time. He took it to the dealership, and they tried to tell him it was normal wear and tear, but the truck only had forty thousand miles on it. Forty thousand! I told him he needed to look up the technical service bulletins, because I guarantee you Ford knew about that issue before they even rolled them off the assembly line. It's like how they build appliances nowadays. My grandmother had a Frigidaire from the 1950s that ran for fifty years. Now you buy a refrigerator and if the ice maker lasts past the warranty, you're lucky. It's planned obsolescence, that's what it is. They want you to have to buy a new one every five years...

But, yeah. Two years and a couple months, roughly. Ever since that mortgage.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Moving slow? Speaking slow? I don't... I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm tired, like I said, but I don't think I'm moving in slow motion or anything. 

It's funny you mention moving slow, though, because it reminds me of this old guy, Arthur, who used to work at the hardware store down on Main Street. He was easily in his eighties, and he shuffled everywhere. You'd ask him where the galvanized screws were, and it would take him ten minutes just to walk you to the aisle. But the thing about Arthur was, he knew exactly where every single item in that store was. You could bring in some obscure, rusted-out plumbing fixture from a house built in 1920, and he'd just squint at it, nod, and shuffle over to some dusty bin in the back and hand you the exact replacement part. They don't make hardware stores like that anymore. Now it's all big box stores with kids working there who don't know a Phillips head from a flathead. I went into Home Depot last month looking for a specific router bit—a half-inch dovetail—and the kid in the tool section looked at me like I was speaking Greek. He tried to point me toward the drill bits. I mean, come on. If you're going to work in the tool department, you should at least know the difference between a drill and a router. It's just basic knowledge. But they don't train anybody anymore. It's all just about getting bodies on the floor to scan barcodes...

But, uh, no. I don't think I'm moving or talking slower. Just regular, I guess.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yeah, most days. I wake up and there's just this heavy, gray feeling already sitting right on my chest. Even when I'm out in the shop, surrounded by all the wood I used to really love working with, it all just feels completely flat. I have to fight the urge to just stand there staring at the wall. 

Speaking of the shop, I was actually just staring at this stack of white oak I got in last month. Beautiful grain on it, quarter-sawn. Quarter-sawn oak is what they used to use for all that old Craftsman style furniture back in the day, you know, Gustav Stickley and all that. It's got these medullary rays—these little flecks or ribbons that catch the light—that you only get when you cut the log at a very specific angle. It's a lot more expensive because there's way more waste when the mill cuts it, but it's incredibly stable. Doesn't warp or cup with humidity like plain-sawn lumber does. I was supposed to build a big dining table out of it for a client. A massive trestle table, ten feet long. The guy wanted it stained dark, which is honestly a crime with white oak, if you ask me. If you want it dark, you're supposed to fume it with ammonia, that's the traditional way. The ammonia fumes react with the natural tannins in the oak and it turns it this rich, deep brown from the inside out. You just can't replicate that depth with a cheap can of Minwax from the hardware store. People just don't understand wood chemistry anymore. They just want to slap a coat of polyurethane on it and call it a day...

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, right, the heavy feeling. Yeah. It's pretty much all day, every day. Just... gray.

Make decisions? I don't think so. I haven't really noticed it being any harder. If something needs deciding, I just pick something. 

Like the hardware for those cabinets I was talking about. I just ordered a box of Blum concealed hinges yesterday and called it a day. Everyone wants soft-close doors now anyway. It's funny how that became the standard. People will slam their car doors, they'll slam the front door, but a kitchen cabinet makes a little "tap" against the frame and suddenly it's a problem. Those soft-close hinges are something else, though. They have this tiny little hydraulic cylinder built right into the metal cup. It's a neat piece of engineering, but man, they are a nightmare to adjust if your cabinet boxes aren't perfectly square. You've got three different adjustment screws on the mounting plate—up and down, left and right, in and out. You turn one a hair too far and the door binds against the next one. 

I kind of miss the old solid brass butt hinges. You had to actually chisel out the mortise by hand with a mallet. It took patience. If you cut it too deep, the door wouldn't close right, and you'd have to shim it with a tiny piece of wood veneer. Now you just drill a big 35-millimeter hole with a Forstner bit, snap the metal hinge in, and twist a screw until it lines up. Anyone can do it. Kind of takes the soul out of the work, honestly... 

But, um... no. Decisions are fine. I just do what I have to do.

Now you buy a refrigerator and if the ice maker lasts past the warranty, you're lucky. It's planned obsolescence, that's what it is. Slowed down? I mean, I don't think so. I'm not moving in slow motion or anything. I still talk the same way I always have, far as I can tell. 

Though, talking about slowing down, you should see the way the new guys on the job site work these days. It's like they've got nowhere to be. We had this kid, maybe twenty-two, supposed to be helping me frame up a partition wall last week. I swear, it took him ten minutes just to measure and cut one stud. And then he pulls out his phone to use the calculator app to figure out half of forty-eight and three-quarters. I mean, come on. When I started out, you didn't need a phone to do basic fraction math in your head. You just learned the marks on the tape. 

And the tools they use now! Everything is battery-powered. Battery-powered nail guns, battery-powered miter saws. They're heavy, they're bulky, and the batteries always die right when you're in the middle of a cut. I still use my old pneumatic framing nailer. Sure, you have to drag an air hose around, but that thing fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, and it never runs out of juice as long as the compressor is running. The sound of a compressor kicking on... that used to mean a good day's work was happening. Now it's just this high-pitched whine from these brushless motors. They don't have the same torque, either. Try driving a three-inch screw into dense old-growth Douglas Fir with one of those little battery impacts. It'll just sit there clicking and chattering, stripping the screw head right out...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, my speech. No, I don't think I'm talking any slower. I just... talk.

I bought it at this little leather shop up in the mountains years ago, back when my ex-wife and I used to go camping up there. The guy who made it hand-tooled the whole thing. You just don't see craftsmanship like that much anymore. Most belts you buy now, even the ones that say \"genuine leather,\" they're just bonded leather. Beautiful grain on it, quarter-sawn. Quarter-sawn oak is what they used to use for all that old Craftsman style furniture back in the day, you know, Gustav Stickley and all that. It's got these medullary rays—these little flecks or ribbons that catch the light—that you only get when you cut the log at a very specific angle. It's a lot more expensive because there's way more waste when the mill cuts it, but it's incredibly stable. Doesn't warp or cup with humidity like plain-sawn lumber does. I was supposed to build a big dining table out of it for a client. A massive trestle table, ten feet long. The guy wanted it stained dark, which is honestly a crime with white oak, if you ask me. If you want it dark, you're supposed to fume it with ammonia, that's the traditional way. The ammonia fumes react with the natural tannins in the oak and it turns it this rich, deep brown from the inside out. You just can't replicate that depth with a cheap can of Minwax from the hardware store. People just don't understand wood chemistry anymore. They just want to slap a coat of polyurethane on it and call it a day...\n\nBut, uh, what were you asking? Oh, right, the heavy feeling. Yeah. It's pretty much all day, every day. Just... gray.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to make decisions than you used to?\n\nPatient: Make decisions? I don't think so. I haven't really noticed it being any harder. If something needs deciding, I just pick something. \n\nLike the hardware for those cabinets I was talking about. I just ordered a box of Blum concealed hinges yesterday and called it a day. Everyone wants soft-close doors now anyway. It's funny how that became the standard. People will slam their car doors, they'll slam the front door, but a kitchen cabinet makes a little \"tap\" against the frame and suddenly it's a problem. Those soft-close hinges are something else, though. They have this tiny little hydraulic cylinder built right into the metal cup. It's a neat piece of engineering, but man, they are a nightmare to adjust if your cabinet boxes aren't perfectly square. You've got three different adjustment screws on the mounting plate—up and down, left and right, in and out. You turn one a hair too far and the door binds against the next one. \n\nI kind of miss the old solid brass butt hinges. You had to actually chisel out the mortise by hand with a mallet. It took patience. If you cut it too deep, the door wouldn't close right, and you'd have to shim it with a tiny piece of wood veneer. Now you just drill a big 35-millimeter hole with a Forstner bit, snap the metal hinge in, and twist a screw until it lines up. Anyone can do it. Kind of takes the soul out of the work, honestly... \n\nBut, um... no. Decisions are fine. I just do what I have to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your movements or speech have slowed down compared to how they used to be?\n\nPatient: Slowed down? I mean, I don't think so. I'm not moving in slow motion or anything. I still talk the same way I always have, far as I can tell. \n\nThough, talking about slowing down, you should see the way the new guys on the job site work these days. It's like they've got nowhere to be. We had this kid, maybe twenty-two, supposed to be helping me frame up a partition wall last week. I swear, it took him ten minutes just to measure and cut one stud. He's standing there with his tape measure, looking at it like he's trying to decipher ancient hieroglyphics. And then he pulls out his phone to use the calculator app to figure out half of forty-eight and three-quarters. I mean, come on. When I started out, you didn't need a phone to do basic fraction math in your head. You just learned the marks on the tape. \n\nAnd the tools they use now! Everything is battery-powered. Battery-powered nail guns, battery-powered miter saws. They're heavy, they're bulky, and the batteries always die right when you're in the middle of a cut. I still use my old pneumatic framing nailer. Sure, you have to drag an air hose around, but that thing fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, and it never runs out of juice as long as the compressor is running. The sound of a compressor kicking on... that used to mean a good day's work was happening. Now it's just this high-pitched whine from these brushless motors. They don't have the same torque, either. Try driving a three-inch screw into dense old-growth Douglas Fir with one of those little battery impacts. It'll just sit there clicking and chattering, stripping the screw head right out...\n\nBut, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, my speech. No, I don't think I'm talking any slower. I just... talk.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. I had this big, red 20-gallon DeWalt compressor for years. Bought it at a pawn shop over in Camden. Guy running the place had a glass eye, I swear. It didn't track right when he looked at you. Anyway, that compressor was a beast, but the regulator valve started sticking on it. You'd turn it on, and it would just hum... this low, vibrating hum that rattled your teeth, but it wouldn't build any pressure. Just sat there using up electricity. I took the whole housing apart trying to fix it. There's this little rubber O-ring inside the manifold that gets brittle if you don't drain the tank regularly. People never drain their tanks, you know? You're supposed to open the petcock at the bottom after every use to let the condensation out, otherwise the inside just rusts to pieces. I knew a guy who had a tank actually blow out on him because the bottom rusted through. Sounded like a shotgun went off in his garage. Blew a hole right through drywall... \n\nBut, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, my energy. Yeah, it's just gone. I just feel wiped out all the time. Like that old compressor, just humming but not doing anything.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about not wanting to live or had thoughts of suicide?\n\nPatient: Suicide? No, no. I haven't... I don't want to kill myself or anything like that. I just... I don't know, sometimes I just wish I could go to sleep and not have to wake up and do it all over again, you know? \n\nSpeaking of sleeping, I bought this new mattress a couple years ago. One of those memory foam things they ship to you in a box. It's crazy how they get a whole king-size mattress rolled up that tight. The delivery guy left it out on the porch, and it weighed a ton. I had to drag it up the stairs by myself. When you cut the plastic off, it just inflates right there in the bedroom. Smelled like chemicals for a week, though. My buddy Dave told me those things off-gas all kinds of toxic stuff. Dave's always reading those conspiracy blogs, though. Last week he was trying to tell me that the government is putting something in the municipal water supply to make the PVC pipes degrade faster so the plumbing unions get more work. I mean, I'm a tradesman, I know how PVC works. It's polyvinyl chloride. It takes like a thousand years to break down in a landfill, a little tap water isn't going to melt it. Dave just has too much time on his hands since he got laid off from the lumber yard... \n\nBut, uh... yeah. I'm not thinking about killing myself. I just... I'm just so tired of feeling like this.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: How long? Well, let's see... it's been going on since I took on the studio mortgage. That was a little over two years ago. I'd say about two years and two months now. \n\nI remember because I signed the papers right around the time the transmission went out on my brother's Ford. He's got this 2015 F-150, the one with the aluminum body. They made a huge deal out of that when it came out, you know, \"military-grade aluminum alloy\" or whatever the commercials said. Supposed to make the truck lighter so it gets better gas mileage, but then they put these tiny little EcoBoost engines in them. Sure, they got twin turbos, but it's still just a V6 trying to pull a full-size truck. Anyway, his transmission started slipping going from third to fourth gear. Just a hard clunk every time. He took it to the dealership, and they tried to tell him it was normal wear and tear, but the truck only had forty thousand miles on it. Forty thousand! I told him he needed to look up the technical service bulletins, because I guarantee you Ford knew about that issue before they even rolled them off the assembly line. It's like how they build appliances nowadays. My grandmother had a Frigidaire from the 1950s that ran for fifty years. Now you buy a refrigerator and if the ice maker lasts past the warranty, you're lucky. It's planned obsolescence, that's what it is. They want you to have to buy a new one every five years...\n\nBut, yeah. Two years and a couple months, roughly. Ever since that mortgage.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving slow? Speaking slow? I don't... I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm tired, like I said, but I don't think I'm moving in slow motion or anything. \n\nIt's funny you mention moving slow, though, because it reminds me of this old guy, Arthur, who used to work at the hardware store down on Main Street. He was easily in his eighties, and he shuffled everywhere. You'd ask him where the galvanized screws were, and it would take him ten minutes just to walk you to the aisle. But the thing about Arthur was, he knew exactly where every single item in that store was. You could bring in some obscure, rusted-out plumbing fixture from a house built in 1920, and he'd just squint at it, nod, and shuffle over to some dusty bin in the back and hand you the exact replacement part. They don't make hardware stores like that anymore. Now it's all big box stores with kids working there who don't know a Phillips head from a flathead. I went into Home Depot last month looking for a specific router bit—a half-inch dovetail—and the kid in the tool section looked at me like I was speaking Greek. He tried to point me toward the drill bits. I mean, come on. If you're going to work in the tool department, you should at least know the difference between a drill and a router. It's just basic knowledge. But they don't train anybody anymore. It's all just about getting bodies on the floor to scan barcodes...\n\nBut, uh, no. I don't think I'm moving or talking slower. Just regular, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, I don't think so. My clothes still fit the same, mostly. My belt's on the same notch it's been on for a while. \n\nSpeaking of belts, I actually need to get a new one. The leather on this one is starting to crack right where the buckle hits. I bought it at this little leather shop up in the mountains years ago, back when my ex-wife and I used to go camping up there. The guy who made it hand-tooled the whole thing. You just don't see craftsmanship like that much anymore. Most belts you buy now, even the ones that say \"genuine leather,\" they're just bonded leather. It's basically leather scraps ground up and glued together, like particle board but for clothes. That's why they start peeling after six months. If you want a real belt, you have to look for \"full-grain\" leather. It's the top layer of the hide, got all the natural grain and strength. I was watching this documentary the other night about how they tan leather in Morocco. They still use these huge stone vats filled with pigeon droppings and natural dyes. It's wild. The guys who work there have to stand waist-deep in it all day. I can't even imagine the smell. Makes me glad I just work with wood, you know? Sawdust smells a lot better than whatever they've got going on in those vats...\n\nBut yeah, no weight loss that I've noticed. I'm pretty much the same size I've always been.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel anxious or worried about things that are happening in your life?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Worried? I mean... I guess I worry about paying the bills, like anybody else. But I wouldn't say I'm, like, pacing the floor or having panic attacks or anything. Just the usual stuff, you know?\n\nThough, speaking of worrying, my neighbor, Dave, he's a worrier. The guy is obsessed with his lawn. I'm talking out there with a ruler measuring the grass blades type of obsessed. He's got this whole irrigation system set up on a timer, and he's constantly tweaking the sprinkler heads. Last week, we had that heavy rain, right? Just a total downpour for two days straight. And I see Dave out there in a raincoat, digging little trenches to make sure the water doesn't pool near his prize-winning azaleas. I tried to tell him, \"Dave, they're plants. They grow in the dirt. They can handle a little water.\" But he wouldn't listen. He started going on about root rot and soil pH levels. It's like, man, if you spend that much time stressing about grass, when do you actually get to enjoy the yard? I built him a nice little cedar bench for his patio a couple years ago. Beautiful piece of wood, Western Red Cedar, naturally rot-resistant. I finished it with a spar urethane so it could handle the weather. He put it out there, but I don't think I've ever actually seen him sit on it. He's always too busy pulling weeds or edging the driveway. It's a shame, really. Cedar has such a nice smell when it warms up in the sun...\n\nBut, uh, me? No, I don't think I'm overly anxious. Just trying to get through the day, mostly.\n\nDoctor: Are these feelings of heaviness and tiredness something you experience for most of the day, every day?\n\nPatient: Yeah, most days. I wake up and there's just this heavy, gray feeling already sitting right on my chest. Even when I'm out in the shop, surrounded by all the wood I used to really love working with, it all just feels completely flat. I have to fight the urge to just stand there staring at the wall. \n\nSpeaking of the shop, I was actually just staring at this stack of white oak I got in last month. Beautiful grain on it, quarter-sawn. Quarter-sawn oak is what they used to use for all that old Craftsman style furniture back in the day, you know, Gustav Stickley and all that. It's got these medullary rays—these little flecks or ribbons that catch the light—that you only get when you cut the log at a very specific angle. It's a lot more expensive because there's way more waste when the mill cuts it, but it's incredibly stable. Doesn't warp or cup with humidity like plain-sawn lumber does. I was supposed to build a big dining table out of it for a client. A massive trestle table, ten feet long. The guy wanted it stained dark, which is honestly a crime with white oak, if you ask me. If you want it dark, you're supposed to fume it with ammonia, that's the traditional way. The ammonia fumes react with the natural tannins in the oak and it turns it this rich, deep brown from the inside out. You just can't replicate that depth with a cheap can of Minwax from the hardware store. People just don't understand wood chemistry anymore. They just want to slap a coat of polyurethane on it and call it a day...\n\nBut, uh, what were you asking? Oh, right, the heavy feeling. Yeah. It's pretty much all day, every day. Just... gray.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to make decisions than you used to?\n\nPatient: Make decisions? I don't think so. I haven't really noticed it being any harder. If something needs deciding, I just pick something. \n\nLike the hardware for those cabinets I was talking about. I just ordered a box of Blum concealed hinges yesterday and called it a day. Everyone wants soft-close doors now anyway. It's funny how that became the standard. People will slam their car doors, they'll slam the front door, but a kitchen cabinet makes a little \"tap\" against the frame and suddenly it's a problem. Those soft-close hinges are something else, though. They have this tiny little hydraulic cylinder built right into the metal cup. It's a neat piece of engineering, but man, they are a nightmare to adjust if your cabinet boxes aren't perfectly square. You've got three different adjustment screws on the mounting plate—up and down, left and right, in and out. You turn one a hair too far and the door binds against the next one. \n\nI kind of miss the old solid brass butt hinges. You had to actually chisel out the mortise by hand with a mallet. It took patience. If you cut it too deep, the door wouldn't close right, and you'd have to shim it with a tiny piece of wood veneer. Now you just drill a big 35-millimeter hole with a Forstner bit, snap the metal hinge in, and twist a screw until it lines up. Anyone can do it. Kind of takes the soul out of the work, honestly... \n\nBut, um... no. Decisions are fine. I just do what I have to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your movements or speech have slowed down compared to how they used to be?\n\nPatient: Slowed down? I mean, I don't think so. I'm not moving in slow motion or anything. I still talk the same way I always have, far as I can tell. \n\nThough, talking about slowing down, you should see the way the new guys on the job site work these days. It's like they've got nowhere to be. We had this kid, maybe twenty-two, supposed to be helping me frame up a partition wall last week. I swear, it took him ten minutes just to measure and cut one stud. He's standing there with his tape measure, looking at it like he's trying to decipher ancient hieroglyphics. And then he pulls out his phone to use the calculator app to figure out half of forty-eight and three-quarters. I mean, come on. When I started out, you didn't need a phone to do basic fraction math in your head. You just learned the marks on the tape. \n\nAnd the tools they use now! Everything is battery-powered. Sure, you have to drag an air hose around, but that thing fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, and it never runs out of juice as long as the compressor is running. The sound of a compressor kicking on... that used to mean a good day's work was happening. Now it's just this high-pitched whine from these brushless motors. They don't have the same torque, either. Initiate tasks? Yeah, I guess so. It's just... I'm so tired all the time. By midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling heavy lumber all day, even if I haven't done much of anything. And even after a full night in bed, I can barely push through the basics—measuring, cutting, returning calls—without feeling completely wiped out. 

Speaking of hauling lumber, you wouldn't believe the price of good plywood these days. It's highway robbery. I had to pick up a few sheets of three-quarter-inch Baltic Birch last week for some shop cabinets. Baltic Birch is the gold standard for drawer boxes, you know. It's got no voids in the inner plies, so the edges look really clean when you sand them down, and it holds screws like nobody's business. But man, the sheet goods market has been a mess ever since the supply chains got all tangled up a couple years ago. Used to be you could get a 5x5 sheet for forty bucks. Now? They want over a hundred. And half the time, the stuff sitting at the lumberyard has been stored wrong, so it's bowed like a banana before you even get it on the truck. 

You really have to watch how you store sheet goods in the shop. If you lean them up against a wall, gravity just takes over and warps them. You've got to lay them flat, or build a proper vertical rack that supports the whole face of the board. I built this rack out of two-by-fours a few years back, put it on heavy-duty casters so I could roll it around the shop. Those casters are great—they have these polyurethane wheels that don't mark up the concrete floor, and they lock down solid when you flip a little lever with your boot. But even with a good rack, moving a full sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself is a surefire way to throw out your back. MDF is so incredibly dense... it's just sawdust and glue pressed together under high heat, so it weighs a ton. Great for making jigs and templates because it's perfectly flat and doesn't have any grain direction, but the dust it makes when you cut it is awful. It's like baby powder. Gets into everything. You absolutely have to wear a good respirator, not just those cheap paper masks...

But, um... yeah. Starting tasks. It's just hard because I'm always so drained.

Pleasure? I... I don't know. Not really, I guess. I just kind of get through the day. Everything just feels kind of flat. 

Like... well, take finishing wood, for example. I used to really enjoy the finishing process. You spend all this time building a piece, getting the joinery tight, sanding it down through the grits—eighty, one-twenty, one-fifty, up to two-twenty. And then you wipe on that first coat of oil, maybe a boiled linseed oil or a tung oil blend, and the grain just pops. It's like the wood comes alive. Especially with something like figured maple, or a nice piece of curly cherry. The chatoyance—that's what they call that optical illusion where the grain looks three-dimensional and shifts when you move around it—it's just incredible. 

But these days, nobody wants an oil finish. They want polyurethane, or worse, they want you to spray it with a tinted lacquer so it looks like it came out of a factory. Spraying lacquer is a whole different beast. You've got to have a dedicated spray booth, explosion-proof exhaust fans, the whole nine yards. The fumes are toxic. And if the humidity is too high, the finish blushes—it traps moisture underneath and turns this milky white color, and then you have to spray a retarder over it to melt it back down and let the moisture escape. It's a headache. I've got this old HVLP spray gun, a Fuji, and it's a great system, really reduces the overspray compared to the old compressor-driven guns. You pour your finish into the cup, adjust the fluid knob, set your fan pattern... horizontal for spraying up and down, vertical for sweeping side to side. You have to keep the gun exactly six inches from the surface and move at a perfectly consistent speed, overlapping your passes by fifty percent. If you hesitate for even a second, you get a run or a sag, and then you're stuck waiting for it to dry so you can sand it out and start over. It's so tedious...

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Enjoying things. No, I don't really get much out of anything lately. It's just work.

I mean, I try to think of something, but my mind just kind of goes blank. It's funny you ask about looking forward to things, though. It reminds me of when I was a kid, maybe eight or nine. My mom would always buy me this huge stick of blue cotton candy right before we got on, which was probably a terrible idea in hindsight. I had this special chamois cloth... you gotta use genuine sheepskin or it leaves streaks on the clear coat, especially on the darker paint. I bought it off this guy at an auto show down in Philly. Huge place, that convention center. I remember they had this one concept car there, doors opened straight up like a spaceship. You see it at a show and then ten years later we're all still pumping regular unleaded. Gas prices are just ridiculous anyway. They want over a hundred. And half the time, the stuff sitting at the lumberyard has been stored wrong, so it's bowed like a banana before you even get it on the truck. \n\nYou really have to watch how you store sheet goods in the shop. If you lean them up against a wall, gravity just takes over and warps them. You've got to lay them flat, or build a proper vertical rack that supports the whole face of the board. Those casters are great—they have these polyurethane wheels that don't mark up the concrete floor, and they lock down solid when you flip a little lever with your boot. Especially with something like figured maple, or a nice piece of curly cherry. The chatoyance—that's what they call that optical illusion where the grain looks three-dimensional and shifts when you move around it—it's just incredible. \n\nBut these days, nobody wants an oil finish. They want polyurethane, or worse, they want you to spray it with a tinted lacquer so it looks like it came out of a factory. Spraying lacquer is a whole different beast. You've got to have a dedicated spray booth, explosion-proof exhaust fans, the whole nine yards. The fumes are toxic. And if the humidity is too high, the finish blushes—it traps moisture underneath and turns this milky white color, and then you have to spray a retarder over it to melt it back down and let the moisture escape. It's a headache. I've got this old HVLP spray gun, a Fuji, and it's a great system, really reduces the overspray compared to the old compressor-driven guns. You pour your finish into the cup, adjust the fluid knob, set your fan pattern... horizontal for spraying up and down, vertical for sweeping side to side. You have to keep the gun exactly six inches from the surface and move at a perfectly consistent speed, overlapping your passes by fifty percent. If you hesitate for even a second, you get a run or a sag, and then you're stuck waiting for it to dry so you can sand it out and start over. It's so tedious...\n\nBut, um... what was I saying? So you have to go back to the architect, pay him another five hundred bucks to adjust the CAD drawings, and start all over. \n\nAnd don't even get me started on the building inspectors. Getting out of bed? Yeah... yeah, it's a struggle. Most days I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling already sitting on me before I even open my eyes. It's like a physical weight. And even when I finally drag myself out to the shop, surrounded by all this wood I used to love working with... it all just feels flat. I literally have to fight not to just stand there staring at it. 

I caught myself doing that yesterday, actually. Just staring at this stack of rough-sawn black walnut I bought off a guy with a portable Wood-Mizer sawmill. Those portable mills are something else, you know? They just tow this big bandsaw rig right onto your property and slice up a felled tree right there in the dirt. But the boards come off rough, so you have to mill them four-square yourself. You can't just run them straight through a thickness planer, either. A lot of guys make that mistake. A planer just makes the top face parallel to the bottom face. If the board is twisted or bowed, the feed rollers just press it flat, the blades cut it, and then it springs right back into a twist when it comes out the other side. You have to run it over a jointer first to get one perfectly flat reference face. 

My jointer is this old eight-inch Delta... weighs about four hundred pounds, solid cast iron beds. I recently upgraded the cutterhead to a helical one with these little square carbide inserts. Best money I ever spent. With the old straight steel knives, if you hit a knot or some tricky grain, you'd get tear-out—these big ugly chunks ripped right out of the surface. And setting those straight knives? A total nightmare. You need a magnetic jig, a dial indicator, and the patience of a saint to get them perfectly level with the outfeed table. But with the helical head, you just screw the inserts in and it slices right through the grain, quiet as a whisper... well, quiet for a machine that eats wood, anyway. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, the mornings. Yeah. It's just that heavy, gray feeling. Makes it really hard to get out of bed and actually turn the machines on.

Sawdust smells a lot better than whatever they've got going on in those vats...\n\nBut yeah, no weight loss that I've noticed. I'm pretty much the same size I've always been.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel anxious or worried about things that are happening in your life?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Worried? I mean... I guess I worry about paying the bills, like anybody else. But I wouldn't say I'm, like, pacing the floor or having panic attacks or anything. Just the usual stuff, you know?\n\nThough, speaking of worrying, my neighbor, Dave, he's a worrier. The guy is obsessed with his lawn. I'm talking out there with a ruler measuring the grass blades type of obsessed. He's got this whole irrigation system set up on a timer, and he's constantly tweaking the sprinkler heads. Last week, we had that heavy rain, right? Just a total downpour for two days straight. And I see Dave out there in a raincoat, digging little trenches to make sure the water doesn't pool near his prize-winning azaleas. I tried to tell him, \"Dave, they're plants. They grow in the dirt. They can handle a little water.\" But he wouldn't listen. He started going on about root rot and soil pH levels. It's like, man, if you spend that much time stressing about grass, when do you actually get to enjoy the yard? I built him a nice little cedar bench for his patio a couple years ago. Beautiful piece of wood, Western Red Cedar, naturally rot-resistant. I finished it with a spar urethane so it could handle the weather. He put it out there, but I don't think I've ever actually seen him sit on it. He's always too busy pulling weeds or edging the driveway. It's a shame, really. Cedar has such a nice smell when it warms up in the sun...\n\nBut, uh, me? No, I don't think I'm overly anxious. Just trying to get through the day, mostly.\n\nDoctor: Are these feelings of heaviness and tiredness something you experience for most of the day, every day?\n\nPatient: Yeah, most days. I wake up and there's just this heavy, gray feeling already sitting right on my chest. Even when I'm out in the shop, surrounded by all the wood I used to really love working with, it all just feels completely flat. I have to fight the urge to just stand there staring at the wall. \n\nSpeaking of the shop, I was actually just staring at this stack of white oak I got in last month. Beautiful grain on it, quarter-sawn. Quarter-sawn oak is what they used to use for all that old Craftsman style furniture back in the day, you know, Gustav Stickley and all that. It's got these medullary rays—these little flecks or ribbons that catch the light—that you only get when you cut the log at a very specific angle. It's a lot more expensive because there's way more waste when the mill cuts it, but it's incredibly stable. Doesn't warp or cup with humidity like plain-sawn lumber does. I was supposed to build a big dining table out of it for a client. A massive trestle table, ten feet long. The guy wanted it stained dark, which is honestly a crime with white oak, if you ask me. If you want it dark, you're supposed to fume it with ammonia, that's the traditional way. The ammonia fumes react with the natural tannins in the oak and it turns it this rich, deep brown from the inside out. You just can't replicate that depth with a cheap can of Minwax from the hardware store. People just don't understand wood chemistry anymore. Just... gray.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to make decisions than you used to?\n\nPatient: Make decisions? I don't think so. I haven't really noticed it being any harder. If something needs deciding, I just pick something. \n\nLike the hardware for those cabinets I was talking about. I just ordered a box of Blum concealed hinges yesterday and called it a day. Everyone wants soft-close doors now anyway. It's funny how that became the standard. People will slam their car doors, they'll slam the front door, but a kitchen cabinet makes a little \"tap\" against the frame and suddenly it's a problem. Those soft-close hinges are something else, though. They have this tiny little hydraulic cylinder built right into the metal cup. It's a neat piece of engineering, but man, they are a nightmare to adjust if your cabinet boxes aren't perfectly square. You've got three different adjustment screws on the mounting plate—up and down, left and right, in and out. It took patience. If you cut it too deep, the door wouldn't close right, and you'd have to shim it with a tiny piece of wood veneer. Now you just drill a big 35-millimeter hole with a Forstner bit, snap the metal hinge in, and twist a screw until it lines up. Anyone can do it. Kind of takes the soul out of the work, honestly... \n\nBut, um... no. Decisions are fine. I just do what I have to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your movements or speech have slowed down compared to how they used to be?\n\nPatient: Slowed down? I mean, I don't think so. And then he pulls out his phone to use the calculator app to figure out half of forty-eight and three-quarters. I mean, come on. When I started out, you didn't need a phone to do basic fraction math in your head. You just learned the marks on the tape. \n\nAnd the tools they use now! Everything is battery-powered. Battery-powered nail guns, battery-powered miter saws. They're heavy, they're bulky, and the batteries always die right when you're in the middle of a cut. I still use my old pneumatic framing nailer. Sure, you have to drag an air hose around, but that thing fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, and it never runs out of juice as long as the compressor is running. The sound of a compressor kicking on... that used to mean a good day's work was happening. Now it's just this high-pitched whine from these brushless motors. They don't have the same torque, either. Try driving a three-inch screw into dense old-growth Douglas Fir with one of those little battery impacts. It'll just sit there clicking and chattering, stripping the screw head right out...\n\nBut, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, my speech. No, I don't think I'm talking any slower. I just... talk.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to initiate activities or tasks than you used to?\n\nPatient: Initiate tasks? Yeah, I guess so. It's just... I'm so tired all the time. By midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling heavy lumber all day, even if I haven't done much of anything. And even after a full night in bed, I can barely push through the basics—measuring, cutting, returning calls—without feeling completely wiped out. \n\nSpeaking of hauling lumber, you wouldn't believe the price of good plywood these days. It's highway robbery. I had to pick up a few sheets of three-quarter-inch Baltic Birch last week for some shop cabinets. Baltic Birch is the gold standard for drawer boxes, you know. It's got no voids in the inner plies, so the edges look really clean when you sand them down, and it holds screws like nobody's business. But man, the sheet goods market has been a mess ever since the supply chains got all tangled up a couple years ago. Used to be you could get a 5x5 sheet for forty bucks. Now? They want over a hundred. And half the time, the stuff sitting at the lumberyard has been stored wrong, so it's bowed like a banana before you even get it on the truck. \n\nYou really have to watch how you store sheet goods in the shop. If you lean them up against a wall, gravity just takes over and warps them. You've got to lay them flat, or build a proper vertical rack that supports the whole face of the board. I built this rack out of two-by-fours a few years back, put it on heavy-duty casters so I could roll it around the shop. Those casters are great—they have these polyurethane wheels that don't mark up the concrete floor, and they lock down solid when you flip a little lever with your boot. But even with a good rack, moving a full sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself is a surefire way to throw out your back. MDF is so incredibly dense... it's just sawdust and glue pressed together under high heat, so it weighs a ton. Great for making jigs and templates because it's perfectly flat and doesn't have any grain direction, but the dust it makes when you cut it is awful. It's like baby powder. Gets into everything. You absolutely have to wear a good respirator, not just those cheap paper masks...\n\nBut, um... yeah. Starting tasks. And then you wipe on that first coat of oil, maybe a boiled linseed oil or a tung oil blend, and the grain just pops. It's like the wood comes alive. Especially with something like figured maple, or a nice piece of curly cherry. The chatoyance—that's what they call that optical illusion where the grain looks three-dimensional and shifts when you move around it—it's just incredible. \n\nBut these days, nobody wants an oil finish. They want polyurethane, or worse, they want you to spray it with a tinted lacquer so it looks like it came out of a factory. Spraying lacquer is a whole different beast. You've got to have a dedicated spray booth, explosion-proof exhaust fans, the whole nine yards. The fumes are toxic. And if the humidity is too high, the finish blushes—it traps moisture underneath and turns this milky white color, and then you have to spray a retarder over it to melt it back down and let the moisture escape. It's a headache. I've got this old HVLP spray gun, a Fuji, and it's a great system, really reduces the overspray compared to the old compressor-driven guns. You pour your finish into the cup, adjust the fluid knob, set your fan pattern... horizontal for spraying up and down, vertical for sweeping side to side. You have to keep the gun exactly six inches from the surface and move at a perfectly consistent speed, overlapping your passes by fifty percent. If you hesitate for even a second, you get a run or a sag, and then you're stuck waiting for it to dry so you can sand it out and start over. It's so tedious...\n\nBut, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Enjoying things. No, I don't really get much out of anything lately. It's just work.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your movements or speech have slowed down compared to how they used to be?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't you... didn't you just ask me that? I'm pretty sure we just talked about this a few minutes ago. No, like I said, I don't think I'm moving or talking any slower than I usually do. I'm just talking normal. \n\nIf you want to see something actually moving slow, though, you should try pulling a building permit down at the city planning office these days. It is absolute molasses. You go in there for a simple alteration permit—maybe you're just putting in a header for a new double-hung window—and they make you jump through hoops like you're building a commercial skyscraper. You pull a ticket, you sit in those hard plastic chairs for two hours, and when they finally call your number, the guy behind the glass tells you your blueprints aren't drawn to the right scale. So you have to go back to the architect, pay him another five hundred bucks to adjust the CAD drawings, and start all over. \n\nAnd don't even get me started on the building inspectors. You finally get the permit, you do all the framing, you call for a rough-in inspection, and the guy shows up three days late. He walks in with his little clipboard, shines his flashlight at the joist hangers, and tells you you used the wrong gauge nails. I've been using Simpson Strong-Tie nails for twenty-five years, I know exactly what the shear strength is on a 10d galvanized nail. But no, he says the new local code requires the structural screws. So you spend all afternoon pulling nails with a cat's paw. You ever use a cat's paw? It's this little pry bar with a V-notch. You hammer it right into the wood under the nail head. It completely ruins the face of the stud, splinters it all to hell, but it's the only way to get a driven framing nail out... \n\nBut, uh, anyway. Sorry. You can't just run them straight through a thickness planer, either. A lot of guys make that mistake. A planer just makes the top face parallel to the bottom face. Taking longer? I mean... I don't think so. I haven't really timed myself or anything. Some things just take a long time no matter what, you know? You can't really rush the work. 

Like... take sharpening chisels. You absolutely cannot rush a good edge on a bench chisel or a hand plane iron. A lot of guys try to save time by using those high-speed bench grinders, but if you're not careful, you overheat the high-carbon steel. The tip turns blue, and boom, you've ruined the temper. The edge will just crumble the next time you hit it with a mallet. You have to use a slow-speed wet grinder, or just do it by hand on water stones. I prefer the stones. You have to flatten the back first—that's crucial, you need a perfectly flat mirror finish on the back before you even touch the bevel. Then you set your primary bevel, usually twenty-five degrees. I use a honing guide, it's this little brass jig with a roller wheel, to keep the angle exactly right. You work your way up the grits... a thousand grit, four thousand, eight thousand. Then you bump the angle up just a couple of degrees for a micro-bevel. Just a few pull strokes on the finest stone. You finish it off by dragging it backward across a leather strop loaded with this green chromium oxide compound. When you're done, you can literally dry-shave the hair off your arm with it. It'll slice through end-grain oak like it's warm butter. But it's a whole process, you know? It can take up half the morning sometimes just getting the blades ready to actually cut anything...

But, uh... I lost my train of thought. Were you asking about my tools? Oh, right, completing tasks. No, I don't think I'm any slower than I used to be. The work just takes what it takes.

And then he pulls out his phone to use the calculator app to figure out half of forty-eight and three-quarters. I mean, come on. When I started out, you didn't need a phone to do basic fraction math in your head. You just learned the marks on the tape. \n\nAnd the tools they use now! Everything is battery-powered. Battery-powered nail guns, battery-powered miter saws. They're heavy, they're bulky, and the batteries always die right when you're in the middle of a cut. I still use my old pneumatic framing nailer. Sure, you have to drag an air hose around, but that thing fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, and it never runs out of juice as long as the compressor is running. The sound of a compressor kicking on... that used to mean a good day's work was happening. Now it's just this high-pitched whine from these brushless motors. They don't have the same torque, either. Try driving a three-inch screw into dense old-growth Douglas Fir with one of those little battery impacts. It'll just sit there clicking and chattering, stripping the screw head right out...\n\nBut, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, my speech. No, I don't think I'm talking any slower. I just... talk.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to initiate activities or tasks than you used to?\n\nPatient: Initiate tasks? Yeah, I guess so. It's just... I'm so tired all the time. By midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling heavy lumber all day, even if I haven't done much of anything. And even after a full night in bed, I can barely push through the basics—measuring, cutting, returning calls—without feeling completely wiped out. \n\nSpeaking of hauling lumber, you wouldn't believe the price of good plywood these days. It's highway robbery. I had to pick up a few sheets of three-quarter-inch Baltic Birch last week for some shop cabinets. Baltic Birch is the gold standard for drawer boxes, you know. It's got no voids in the inner plies, so the edges look really clean when you sand them down, and it holds screws like nobody's business. But man, the sheet goods market has been a mess ever since the supply chains got all tangled up a couple years ago. Used to be you could get a 5x5 sheet for forty bucks. Now? They want over a hundred. And half the time, the stuff sitting at the lumberyard has been stored wrong, so it's bowed like a banana before you even get it on the truck. \n\nYou really have to watch how you store sheet goods in the shop. If you lean them up against a wall, gravity just takes over and warps them. You've got to lay them flat, or build a proper vertical rack that supports the whole face of the board. I built this rack out of two-by-fours a few years back, put it on heavy-duty casters so I could roll it around the shop. Those casters are great—they have these polyurethane wheels that don't mark up the concrete floor, and they lock down solid when you flip a little lever with your boot. But even with a good rack, moving a full sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself is a surefire way to throw out your back. MDF is so incredibly dense... it's just sawdust and glue pressed together under high heat, so it weighs a ton. Great for making jigs and templates because it's perfectly flat and doesn't have any grain direction, but the dust it makes when you cut it is awful. It's like baby powder. Gets into everything. You absolutely have to wear a good respirator, not just those cheap paper masks...\n\nBut, um... yeah. Starting tasks. You spend all this time building a piece, getting the joinery tight, sanding it down through the grits—eighty, one-twenty, one-fifty, up to two-twenty. And then you wipe on that first coat of oil, maybe a boiled linseed oil or a tung oil blend, and the grain just pops. It's like the wood comes alive. Especially with something like figured maple, or a nice piece of curly cherry. The chatoyance—that's what they call that optical illusion where the grain looks three-dimensional and shifts when you move around it—it's just incredible. \n\nBut these days, nobody wants an oil finish. They want polyurethane, or worse, they want you to spray it with a tinted lacquer so it looks like it came out of a factory. Spraying lacquer is a whole different beast. You've got to have a dedicated spray booth, explosion-proof exhaust fans, the whole nine yards. The fumes are toxic. And if the humidity is too high, the finish blushes—it traps moisture underneath and turns this milky white color, and then you have to spray a retarder over it to melt it back down and let the moisture escape. It's a headache. I've got this old HVLP spray gun, a Fuji, and it's a great system, really reduces the overspray compared to the old compressor-driven guns. You pour your finish into the cup, adjust the fluid knob, set your fan pattern... horizontal for spraying up and down, vertical for sweeping side to side. You have to keep the gun exactly six inches from the surface and move at a perfectly consistent speed, overlapping your passes by fifty percent. If you hesitate for even a second, you get a run or a sag, and then you're stuck waiting for it to dry so you can sand it out and start over. It's so tedious...\n\nBut, um... what was I saying? You pull a ticket, you sit in those hard plastic chairs for two hours, and when they finally call your number, the guy behind the glass tells you your blueprints aren't drawn to the right scale. So you have to go back to the architect, pay him another five hundred bucks to adjust the CAD drawings, and start all over. \n\nAnd don't even get me started on the building inspectors. You finally get the permit, you do all the framing, you call for a rough-in inspection, and the guy shows up three days late. He walks in with his little clipboard, shines his flashlight at the joist hangers, and tells you you used the wrong gauge nails. I've been using Simpson Strong-Tie nails for twenty-five years, I know exactly what the shear strength is on a 10d galvanized nail. But no, he says the new local code requires the structural screws. So you spend all afternoon pulling nails with a cat's paw. You ever use a cat's paw? It's this little pry bar with a V-notch. You hammer it right into the wood under the nail head. It completely ruins the face of the stud, splinters it all to hell, but it's the only way to get a driven framing nail out... \n\nBut, uh, anyway. Sorry. I literally have to fight not to just stand there staring at it. \n\nI caught myself doing that yesterday, actually. Just staring at this stack of rough-sawn black walnut I bought off a guy with a portable Wood-Mizer sawmill. Those portable mills are something else, you know? They just tow this big bandsaw rig right onto your property and slice up a felled tree right there in the dirt. But the boards come off rough, so you have to mill them four-square yourself. You can't just run them straight through a thickness planer, either. A lot of guys make that mistake. A planer just makes the top face parallel to the bottom face. If the board is twisted or bowed, the feed rollers just press it flat, the blades cut it, and then it springs right back into a twist when it comes out the other side. You have to run it over a jointer first to get one perfectly flat reference face. \n\nMy jointer is this old eight-inch Delta... weighs about four hundred pounds, solid cast iron beds. I recently upgraded the cutterhead to a helical one with these little square carbide inserts. Best money I ever spent. With the old straight steel knives, if you hit a knot or some tricky grain, you'd get tear-out—these big ugly chunks ripped right out of the surface. And setting those straight knives? A total nightmare. You need a magnetic jig, a dial indicator, and the patience of a saint to get them perfectly level with the outfeed table. But with the helical head, you just screw the inserts in and it slices right through the grain, quiet as a whisper... well, quiet for a machine that eats wood, anyway. \n\nBut, um... what were we talking about? Oh, the mornings. Yeah. It's just that heavy, gray feeling. You absolutely cannot rush a good edge on a bench chisel or a hand plane iron. A lot of guys try to save time by using those high-speed bench grinders, but if you're not careful, you overheat the high-carbon steel. The tip turns blue, and boom, you've ruined the temper. The edge will just crumble the next time you hit it with a mallet. You have to use a slow-speed wet grinder, or just do it by hand on water stones. I prefer the stones. You have to flatten the back first—that's crucial, you need a perfectly flat mirror finish on the back before you even touch the bevel. Then you set your primary bevel, usually twenty-five degrees. I use a honing guide, it's this little brass jig with a roller wheel, to keep the angle exactly right. You work your way up the grits... a thousand grit, four thousand, eight thousand. Then you bump the angle up just a couple of degrees for a micro-bevel. Just a few pull strokes on the finest stone. You finish it off by dragging it backward across a leather strop loaded with this green chromium oxide compound. When you're done, you can literally dry-shave the hair off your arm with it. It'll slice through end-grain oak like it's warm butter. But it's a whole process, you know? It can take up half the morning sometimes just getting the blades ready to actually cut anything...\n\nBut, uh... I lost my train of thought. Were you asking about my tools? Oh, right, completing tasks. No, I don't think I'm any slower than I used to be. The work just takes what it takes."
